Автор: Financial Times

Welcome to your Editor’s Choice on what has been one of the busiest weeks of the year, with three elections in Brazil, Serbia and Israel, and, most importantly, the unveiling of the UK Budget. Readers outside the UK may be baffled by the spectacle that is our Budget, a perfectly choreographed show that has the whole nation holding its breath. The newsroom is buzzing on Budget day, with reporters and editors huddled around the main news desk to listen to the chancellor deliver his speech, and then to our economics editor share his main takeaways. It is also the only day of the year when we publish two newspapers in the UK, including a full print Budget supplement with its own front page.  So what about the Budget? It was, as we wrote in our FT View, a Budget designed to buy time and delay the hard decisions. Instead of a decisive plan to cut the welfare bill, boost defence spending and spur growth, chancellor John Healey made only modest commitments on tax and spending, including a £100 handout to help households with winter energy bills. Our crack team of reporters and columnists answer the big questions about the Budget on Political Fix. For more on what the Budget means for your money, read our full breakdown here. And with inflation on the up and tax thresholds still frozen, use our new fiscal drag calculator to find out how much more tax you could be paying in the years ahead. My choices this week We finally got our hands on Anthropic’s IPO prospectus on Monday. And it didn’t disappoint. From $800bn in data centre commitments to an extraordinary governance structure, we learnt a lot from the 240,000-word document. But as our tech writer Richard Waters points out, it’s what isn’t in the listing that points to some of the biggest questions about Anthropic’s business and the wider AI sector. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made a stunning comeback in Brazil’s presidential election run-off last Sunday, beating rival Flávio Bolsonaro (who subsequently fled to the US). Lula’s victory is surely his greatest political triumph. But his re-election has also triggered a powerful market rout. Eighty-one-year-old Lula has a fiscal reckoning on his hands. Israel’s election delivered a far less decisive outcome than those in Brazil and Serbia (where Aleksandar Vučić was ousted after 12 years in charge).
